Security Alert

Critical PHP Flaws Leaked Before Embargo

Reporting by Sebastix and sudocarlos

Two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP were leaked hours before their scheduled embargo lift, forcing administrators across the web to prepare emergency countermeasures. Sebastix flagged the breach from security disclosures: In the last hour, two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP have been leaked. These vulnerabilities were previously scheduled under embargo and due for release on Thursday at 11 am ET, prompting warnings across developer channels. sudocarlos urged operators to ready their servers immediately: All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available.

Identity & Authentication

SMS Verification Under Fire

Advisory from Foundation

The persistent hazard of SIM swapping drew a sharp reminder from hardware manufacturer Foundation, who warned that phone numbers provide an illusion of security: Your phone number is a terrible second factor. When an attacker co-opts a mobile carrier account, incoming verification codes divert directly to the attacker. Users are urged to migrate accounts to authenticator keys, enforce carrier port-out PIN locks, and strip carrier phone numbers from recovery options.

Dispatches from State College

Builders in a Bear Market

At Happy Valley Brewing Company, Nostr developers face down slow growth with working software, web-of-trust search, and an alliance against platform giants.

Dispatch by Derek Ross · State College, Pennsylvania

A room full of software engineers and protocol architects gathered at the Happy Valley Brewing Company in Pennsylvania for the third annual Nostr Valley conference, confronting an industry slowdown with working code rather than pitch decks. Writing in a comprehensive retrospective of the gathering, organizer Derek Ross refused to sugarcoat the prevailing climate: It's a bear market for Nostr, and nobody in the room pretended otherwise. User growth has moderated, speculative funding has evaporated, and marginal projects have shuttered over the preceding twelve months. Yet the mood inside the hall was defined by pragmatic maturation rather than retreat.

The dominant consensus across eight lectures and an afternoon panel was a collective departure from protocol evangelism: stop asking people to care about the protocol. Keynote presenter Seth, recounting lessons from food application Zap Cooking, noted that pitching cryptographic primitives like Lightning Network identifiers or NIP specifications had created needless consumer friction. Rebranding around culinary community, Zap Cooking integrated passkeys and Google authentication to onboard mainstream households before introducing self-custody rails. As Seth put it: software is not a moat. Brand, curation, relationships and trust are.

Technical demonstrations highlighted how portable identity transforms utility without requiring users to navigate relay mechanics. David Strayhorn demonstrated Brainstorm—the search engine powering today's edition lens—locating decentralized recipes through organic social endorsements rather than corporate indexes. Arkinox unveiled Fanfares, an infrastructure allowing creators to monetize exclusive content through Cashu ecash splits distributed directly over ordinary web links on YouTube. Meanwhile, client resilience emerged as an urgent priority. The Daniel introduced Lazarus, an open specification engineered to recover lost contact lists, mutes, and bookmarks from relay history after client malfunctions: Nobody else has to deal with this shit. Only Nostr has to deal with this stuff. So we're all in it together.

Closing the gathering, Ross proposed forming an Open Handset Alliance for independent applications, inviting non-Nostr products ranking between positions 75 and 100 on mobile app charts to adopt Nostr as shared backend infrastructure against entrenched platform monopolies.

Capital & Compute

The AI Buildout’s Bitcoin Problem

GPU-backed debt piles into warehouses as data center energization lags.

Analysis by TFTC

The frenzied multi-billion-dollar race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure is colliding with fundamental physical and financial limits, mirroring the catastrophic leverage cycle that struck cryptocurrency miners two years ago. In an incisive market memo, TFTC observed: The AI buildout has a bitcoin mining problem.

Hyperscalers and venture-backed compute brokers have accumulated massive debt facilities collateralized against specialized silicon: GPUs are sitting in warehouses waiting for power. GPU-collateralized debt is piling up. Credit markets are flinching. With CoreWeave carrying billions in borrowing and enterprise operators acquiring chips that sit idle awaiting utility interconnects, capital markets are beginning to reassess demand curves. Crucially, whereas Bitcoin miners faced an automated difficulty adjustment every two weeks to purge insolvent operations, the artificial intelligence sector enjoys no such automatic governor: Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment flushes out the overleveraged every two weeks. AI has no such mechanism.

Micro-Commerce

TollGate Drops MAC Trust

Release by TollGate

Open-source gateway project TollGate released version 0.6.0 of its captive WiFi module, overhauling client accounting to bind network access directly to TCP sockets rather than spoofable hardware identifiers: Identity is the TCP socket. No more trusting client-claimed MACs — forged identities can't borrow your session, and MAC rotation can't reset the meter or stretch paid time. The daemon incorporates Cashu ecash settlement with fail-safe balance protection: A payment refused during a mint outage never burns your token.

Reflections

The Internet Used to Be a Home

Curated by Gigi

Reflecting on exhibits from Dutch Design Week, Gigi resurfaced a fundamental question regarding digital life: When was the last time you felt at home on the internet? The proliferation of engagement-maximizing feeds and platform silos has displaced the calm of earlier networks. As highlighted in Gigi's digest selections: The internet now feels rushed and overwhelming but it was never designed this way. It used to be a place where you could go to and leave whenever you wanted.
